To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the fibrillar structure of fibronectin (an extracellular matrix protein) is important for cell differentiation.

1) FN adsorption onto PEA triggers its fibrillar organization into a physiological network, 2) the material-driven fibrillogenesis process is independent of the topography of the material, and 3) the biological activity of the FN network depends on its fibrillar architecture and not on its density.

the fibrillar structure of adsorbed fibronectin on poly(ethyl acrate) is essential to the myogenic differentiation of myoblasts, while the non-fibrillar structure of fibronectin adsorbed on poly(methyl acryate) is not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of material properties on cell differentiation, with the ultimate aim of developing biomimetic scaffolds to control tissue formation.
the design of biomaterials for the control of cell fate.
the effect of topological cues in modulating material driven FN assembly and myogenic differentiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the topological cues can be more important than the chemical cues, especially in the case of electrospun fibers.
material-driven cell responses are dictated by the interplay between the chemical and physical properties of the biomaterials.
the topological cue is a more powerful cue than the chemical cue in the context of the material-driven FN fibrillar assembly and the subsequent myogenic differentiation process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the material-driven FN fibrillar network formation is a key factor to promote cell differentiation.
the material-driven FN fibrillar network formation is not only dependent on material chemistry, but also on topological cues.

material-driven FN fibrillar assembly is a complex process, which involves not only the chemical composition but also the topography of the material surface, which in turn influences cell differentiation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the material-driven FN fibrillar assembly is a complex phenomenon, which depends on both the material chemistry and topology, and that the material-driven assembly of a physiological FN matrix may not always result in a favorable environment for cell adhesion and differentiation.
topography can be used to control the material-driven assembly of proteins and the biological response of cells.
the material-driven FN organization into fibrils can be controlled by the topological features of the material interface.
